paragraphs.text: Ask for the time with {{de:Wie spät ist es?}} or {{de:Wie viel Uhr ist es?}} — both are everyday, both are correct. The answer is built from three pieces: a number, a direction, and the word {{de:Uhr}} when you give an exact hour.

The direction is where English and German part company. {{de:nach}} counts forward from the full hour, {{de:vor}} counts back to the next one, and {{de:halb}} does not mean half past — it names the hour you are heading towards. So {{de:halb acht}} is 7:30, half an hour before eight. Notice the phrase the book drills: {{de:fünf nach halb acht}} and {{de:fünf vor halb acht}} work the same way, stepping five minutes either side of that halfway point.
zehn nach sieben · Viertel nach sieben · zwanzig nach sieben · fünf vor halb acht · halb acht · fünf nach halb acht · Viertel vor acht · kurz vor sieben

Two registers sit side by side. Spoken German prefers the {{de:vor}}/{{de:nach}} system; timetables, appointments and official notices write the digital form. At 14:45 you say {{de:Es ist Viertel vor drei}} to a friend and {{de:Es ist vierzehn Uhr fünfundvierzig}} in an email. Learn both, and know which room you are in.

paragraphs.text: The mistake everyone makes at first is reading {{de:halb acht}} as 8:30. It is not. German {{de:halb}} points forward to the coming hour, so 7:30 is {{de:halb acht}} and 8:30 is {{de:halb neun}}. Say the hour out loud as you look at a clock and the pattern settles quickly.

One more habit worth building now: when you note down an appointment, write the digital form next to the German one. Ten minutes of that and {{de:fünf vor halb acht}} stops being a puzzle and starts being 7:25.
